cards.title: Sequence the email system as a connected chain, not isolated tactics
cards.summary: Build ecommerce email in a dependency order where signup feeds flows, flows capture intent, campaigns create momentum, tests sharpen winners and deliverability keeps it all reaching the inbox.
cards.use_when: When planning the next quarter of email work or deciding which email project to start next in an ecommerce store.
steps: Start with list growth: the source argues that without a steady stream of new subscribers every other email effort operates on a shrinking audience, so fix signup capture before adding complexity elsewhere.
Layer the five core flows next: welcome, browse abandonment, abandoned cart, abandoned checkout and post-purchase. These capture existing intent rather than trying to manufacture it.
Add campaigns after flows: campaigns create momentum with your list, but they work better when triggered flows are already catching high-intent behaviour.
Add A/B testing only on top of already-working elements; the source frames testing as sharpening what works, not as a rescue tool for broken flows.
Layer segmentation to keep sends relevant, then treat deliverability as the foundation that decides whether any of it reaches the inbox.
Use AI last, as an execution accelerator across the whole system rather than a replacement for the structure.
Work through the sections one at a time as a buildout roadmap instead of implementing everything at once.
caveats: The source is a course summary from an agency that also sells buildout services; the sequencing is the presenter's framework, not a measured benchmark.
Stores with a large existing list but weak capture may reasonably prioritise flows over list growth.

cards.title: Audit your email program against the six-layer dependency model
cards.summary: Use a six-layer checklist (signup, flows, campaigns, testing, segmentation, deliverability) to find the weakest link limiting email revenue.
cards.use_when: When email revenue has plateaued and you need to diagnose which stage of the ecommerce email program to invest in next.
steps: List the six layers: list growth/signup forms, core triggered flows, campaigns, A/B testing, segmentation and deliverability.
For each layer, record whether it exists, how it is performing and whether the layer above it depends on it.

Look for breaks in the chain: signup forms feeding flows, flows capturing intent, campaigns creating momentum, tests sharpening winners, segmentation keeping messages relevant and deliverability getting mail to the inbox.
Prioritise the earliest broken link, because later layers inherit problems from earlier ones; a great campaign calendar wastes effort if subscribers are not being captured or mail is not landing.
Implement fixes sequentially rather than simultaneously so you can tell what changed outcomes.
Expect the payoff to be a cleaner system with better timing and more relevant messaging, not simply a higher volume of sends.
caveats: This is the presenter's diagnostic framing from an email course, not a validated scoring model; treat layer priority as a judgement call for your store.
If you sell agency services or build systems for clients, this audit works the same way for a client account, but the source's own pitch to book a buildout call is not a required step.

The welcome flow, browse abandonment flow, abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, and post purchase. Then we layered on campaigns, AB testing, segmentation, and deliverability. And we finished with how to use AI to make the whole system faster and smarter working for you. If there's one takeaway if you want to leave with, it's this. Email performs best when each part supports the next. Your signup forms feed your flows. Your flows capture intent. Your campaigns create momentum. Your AB tests sharpen what's already working. Your segmentation keeps everything relevant. And your deliverability makes sure the whole machine actually reaches the inbox. And finally, AI helps you execute all of it without burning out. So if you implement this properly, you won't just have more emails going out.

 You have a cleaner email system, better timing, more relevant messaging, and a stronger foundation for long-term e-commerce growth.
